In summary, Task 7 completed the engineering groundwork for physical and control- system modifications required to enable future GFM operation. While construction and implementation activities were outside the scope of BP1, this task ensured that all site prerequisites were identified, documented, and ready for execution in subsequent phases of the project. The work ensures that once hardware commissioning begins, plant modifications can proceed efficiently and with reduced technical and operational risk. 7.8 Task 8 - Modeling, Simulation, and Validation for System-Level Studies Task 8 advanced the project’s system-level understanding of how grid-forming (GFM) and grid-following (GFL) resources interact within the Wheatridge hybrid facility and the broader transmission system. Building on the EMT, HIL, and performance-metric foundations developed in earlier tasks, this effort focused on validating mixed GFM/GFL behavior under realistic network conditions, identifying multi-resource interaction modes, and establishing the modeling practices needed to support future commissioning and field demonstration activities. A central element of Task 8 was the execution of a structured series of system-level EMT studies using the generic hybrid-plant model developed in Task 3. These studies evaluated GFM performance under a variety of representative operating scenarios, including voltage depressions, frequency excursions, phase-angle disturbances, and weak-grid conditions consistent with the site’s location on the regional transmission system. Simulations were performed with different combinations of GFM BESS, GFM wind, GFL wind, and solar resources to assess how plant-level supervisory controls, inverter-level droops, and current-limiting behaviors interact during transient events. The results confirmed that GFM-enabled resources demonstrated enhanced angle- stability support, more predictable current-limiting behavior, and stronger voltage and frequency recovery across a broader range of system strengths than comparable GFL resources. The studies also highlighted the importance of coordinated tuning across inverter types: while individual GFM devices performed as expected, system-level behavior was strongly shaped by plant-level voltage and frequency hierarchies, mode transitions, and dispatch-coordination assumptions. These findings directly informed the tuning methodologies and commissioning dependencies documented in Tasks 2 and 6. In addition to hybrid-plant validation, Task 8 evaluated how GFM behavior influences system-level dynamics relevant to regional transmission planning. This included Page 21 of 36 Award Number: DE-EE0010651 Recipient Name: Portland General Electric assessment of fault-response characteristics, short-circuit behavior, dynamic recovery trajectories, and interactions with remote GFL resources across low-SCR network conditions. The studies demonstrated that GFM controls can provide meaningful stabilizing contributions, such as improved phase-angle synchronization and reduced sensitivity to PLL-driven oscillations, when integrated into a hybrid plant operating on a relatively weak transmission corridor. These insights support future incorporation of GFM capabilities into planning-level models and studies. The task also established the workflow for positive-sequence validation that aligns EMT behavior with planning-model assumptions. While EMT simulations were used to characterize detailed GFM behaviors such as angle-persistence, voltage- strengthening, and current-limit dynamics, positive-sequence models were benchmarked against these EMT results to ensure consistency during voltage and frequency events.
